_about: Ground truth from space missions and meteorite analogs. Every statement carries its evidence level and a published reference. Hand-curated; check before citing.

facts.text: Sample returned to Earth on 24 Sep 2023 (121.6 g).
facts.ref: Lauretta et al. 2024, Meteoritics & Planetary Science 59

facts.text: Rich in carbon, nitrogen and hydrated phyllosilicates (serpentine, smectite); similar to but distinct from CI chondrites.
Bulk density 1.19 g/cm3: a porous rubble pile.
Hydrated minerals hold chemically bound water; this does not imply ice or extractable free water.
Samples (5.4 g) returned in Dec 2020; chemical composition similar to CI chondrites.
Dominated by phyllosilicates, carbonates and magnetite formed by aqueous alteration.
Particles returned in 2010 are consistent with thermally metamorphosed LL ordinary chondrites.
Bulk density ~3.9 g/cm3; candidate exposed metallic core or metal-silicate mixture.
facts.ref: Shepard et al. 2021, Planetary Science Journal 2, 125

facts.text: The actual composition (metal fraction) is unknown until the mission arrives.
X-ray and gamma-ray spectroscopy consistent with ordinary chondrites (with surface sulfur depletion).
facts.ref: Nittler et al. 2001, Meteoritics & Planetary Science 36

facts.text: The DART impact (26 Sep 2022) shortened Dimorphos' orbital period by ~33 min.
S-type spectrum consistent with L/LL ordinary chondrites.
facts.ref: Rivkin et al. 2023, Planetary Science Journal

facts.text: Parent body of the HED meteorites (howardites, eucrites, diogenites); differentiated body with a core.
facts.ref: De Sanctis et al. 2012, Science 336; Russell et al. 2012, Science 336

facts.text: Ammoniated phyllosilicates on the surface; carbonate deposits in Occator crater.
facts.ref: De Sanctis et al. 2015, Nature 528; De Sanctis et al. 2016, Nature 536
